title: Repurposing the Pixel Wise T-Test for Wildfire Damage Detection
text:
NOTE: This project uses Google Earth Engine. You will have to code. It is a great opportunity to learn to code, as most of the code is already provided. You will just need to modify it. Some experience with Python would be helpful, but i guess you can like, learn by doing!, or whatever. I will provide a fair amount of guidance on theis if needed. It is possible that if done well this could be turned into a publication


The purpose of this project is to determine whether the Pixel-Wise T-Test (PWTT), originally developed by Ollie Ballinger, for damage detection in war zones, can be adapted to post-fire structure-damage screening in the wildland-urban interface.
PWTT detects abrupt changes in Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) backscatter from the Sentinel-1 satellites. It does not directly see damage. In urban warfare, abrupt SAR change near buildings is often a reasonable proxy for structural destruction. In WUI fires, the interpretation is less direct because houses, trees, shrubs, vehicles, fences, and bare ground are often mixed inside the same 10 m Sentinel-1 pixels.
This project will use Google Earth Engine. This is the most practical way to avoid building a local Sentinel-1 processing pipeline, which is beyond what is reasonable to expect in this course. This is being carried out, not necessarily to prove that radar can replace visual interpretation, or deep learning algorithms, but rather to test whether this simple and easily reproducible change statistic can help identify buildings or neighborhoods that should receive closer review after a wildfire.
This makes the wildfire application interesting because:

Burned vegetation near a house may be correlated with structure loss.
Burned vegetation near a house may create false positives.
Small homes may occupy less than one Sentinel-1 pixel.
Tree canopy can obscure or dominate the radar response.
Suppression activity, debris removal, wet soil, and post-fire cleanup can also change backscatter.

The study question is:

Can the Pixel-Wise T-Test identify burned or destroyed structures in a context where they are surrounded by other abrupt post-fire changes, e.g. burned vegetation?




By the end of the project, students should be able to:

Explain the PWTT algorithm in plain language.
Run a reproducible Earth Engine damage-detection workflow.
Choose defensible pre-fire and post-fire time windows.
Attach raster change scores to building footprints.
Evaluate precision, recall, false positives, and false negatives against reference labels.
Explain how WUI vegetation complicates building-damage interpretation.
Make a clear recommendation about whether PWTT is useful for wildfire response.




Read:

Ballinger, O. 2025. Open access battle damage detection via Pixel-Wise T-Test on Sentinel-1 imagery. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2025.115025
PWTT GitHub repository: https://github.com/oballinger/PWTT
Google Earth Engine Sentinel-1 guide: https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/guides/sentinel1

Use the PWTT repository as a starting point.



Select three to five wildfires and corresponding AOIs in WUI areas with known structure damage. Good candidates are events with public structure-damage maps, or well-documented post-fire imagery that you can annotate. I will help this.
Minimum scope:

three wildfires.
Three communities or bounded WUI AOIs.
Approximately 500-5,000 building footprints.
One reference label set for validation.

The event should have enough damaged and undamaged buildings to make precision and recall meaningful. Avoid AOIs where nearly every building burned or where almost no buildings burned (A ~ 50/50 split would be ideal).
You can use the code from the GitHub repo as a starting point. Make reasonable changes such as renaming variables in your notebook or comments so the workflow refers to fire dates rather than war dates.


Stratification should be based on pre-fire vegetation and land-cover context, not on the PWTT output itself. The goal is to ask where PWTT works well or fails and why. For example, are false positives concentrated around intact houses with burned vegetation nearby.
Create one table with one row per building (buildings from all fires/AOIs are pooled here). Before running the final accuracy assessment, attach context variables to each building footprint:
building_id
damage_label
PWTT_T_mean
PWTT_T_max
PWTT_ring_10_30m
pre_fire_tree_cover_30m
pre_fire_NDVI_30m
landcover_class
dNBR_30m
prediction
Determine vegetation characteristics within rings around each (labeled) building. You can decide on the ring size. Some suggestions to consider:

Building footprint: likely structure signal.
0-10 m ring: immediate defensible-space context (and ~ pixel size).
10-30 m ring: near-structure vegetation and parcel fuels.
30-100 m ring: neighborhood fuel context.

Then divide buildings into a small number of pre-fire context classes (and join to table discussed above). Keep the categories simple enough that each group still has enough damaged and undamaged buildings for evaluation, e.g.:
low vegetation near building
moderate vegetation near building
high vegetation near building
tree-dominated
shrub-dominated
grass-dominated
dense built-up
For each stratum, report precision, recall, F1, and the number of damaged and undamaged buildings. The writeup should explicitly compare error patterns across strata. For example, if precision drops sharply in high-tree-cover parcels, that is evidence that PWTT is responding to vegetation change as well as structure change.






Use Earth Engine’s COPERNICUS/S1_GRD_FLOAT collection through the PWTT code. Earth Engine provides calibrated, orthorectified Sentinel-1 GRD imagery and metadata making it easy to filter and use.
Recommended settings:

Polarizations: VV and VH.
Instrument mode: IW.

(Also, be a ble to explain what these terms mean) only as a comparison.



Use one of these approaches:

Default: Microsoft Building Footprints in Earth Engine or another already available GEE asset.
Preferred: Overture buildings exported to GeoPackage/GeoJSON/GeoParquet and uploaded as a GEE table asset.

Overture releases are definitely available for summer 2026 fires. Old releases are not available indefinitely. Overture’s public release retention is limited, but may be available from mirrors such as Fused. If using Overture, record:
overture_release
download_date
AOI
query_or_udf
source_url_or_path
schema_version_if_known
I will help you with using Overture.



Validation labels may come from:

Official structure-damage inspections.
Manually interpreting high-resolution pre/post imagery.
Existing disaster datasets such as xBD, if the selected fire is included.

Every label must distinguish at least:
destroyed_or_major_damage
not_destroyed
uncertain
not_visible
footprint_mismatch
For model evaluation, collapse labels to binary (destroyed, not destroyed) only after removing or separately reporting uncertain, not_visible, and footprint_mismatch.



The PWTT code masks results using Dynamic World built probability. This is reasonable for dense urban battle damage but not likely to work well in WUI settings.

Try changing the threshold for Dynamic World built probability so that does not discard mixed vegetation-building pixels near homes.
Try making a mask(or masks) based on density of structures in the buildings layer.




Reduce the PWTT raster to building footprints.
At minimum, calculate:
building_id
T_mean
T_max
p_value_mean
n_pre
n_post
damage_prediction
building_area
Also calculate a nearby vegetation/context score:
T_ring_10_30m
dNBR_or_NBR_change
pre_fire_tree_or_vegetation_fraction
distance_to_fire_perimeter
The ring statistic is important because it helps distinguish “the building changed” from “the vegetation around the building changed.”



Do not assume the battle-damage threshold works for wildfire.
Evaluate at least four thresholds:
T > 2.0
T > 3.3
T > 4.0
T > 5.0
Then choose a recommended wildfire threshold based on the precision-recall tradeoff. For screening, high recall may be acceptable. For public damage counts, precision matters more.



Compare predictions to reference labels at the building level.
Report:

Confusion matrix.
Precision.
Recall.
F1.
AUC or precision-recall curve if using continuous T_statistic.
Accuracy by building size class.
Accuracy by vegetation context class.
At least 10 mapped false positives and 10 mapped false negatives. ( As an Appendix)

For the false positives, classify likely causes:
burned vegetation near intact building
building footprint offset
small ancillary structure
post-fire cleanup or debris movement
shadow/layover/topography
actual damage missed in reference labels
other_or_unknown






Submit a notebook that:

Authenticates to Earth Engine.
Defines the AOI and dates.
Runs PWTT or a clearly documented adaptation.
Attaches scores to building footprints.
Exports a table of building-level results.
Produces maps of T_statistic, predicted damage, and validation labels.




Submit a CSV or GeoPackage with:
building_id
geometry_or_centroid
building_source
building_source_release_or_date
T_mean
T_max
T_ring_10_30m
dNBR_or_NBR_change
label
prediction
threshold
notes



The report should include:

Event and AOI description.
Data sources and dates.
Method summary.
Threshold comparison.
Validation metrics.
Error analysis focused on WUI vegetation.
Recommendation: useful, useful only for emergency, or not useful for this fire.




Presentation should include at least:

One slide explaining PWTT.
One map of the (each) AOI and buildings.
One map of PWTT scores.
One validation figure or table.
One slide on false positives/false negatives.
One final recommendation.






Reproducible workflow- Notebook runs, dates/AOI are explicit, exports are documented.
Data provenance- Building, imagery, label, and release metadata are recorded.
PWTT adaptation- Uses PWTT correctly and addresses WUI-specific masking/vegetation issues.
Validation- Metrics are correct, thresholds are compared, uncertainty is handled honestly.
Error analysis- False positives and false negatives are mapped and interpreted.
Communication- Report and presentation make a clear, evidence-based recommendation.

title: Repurposing the Pixel Wise T-Test for Wildfire Damage Detection
text:
Reproducible workflow- Notebook runs, dates/AOI are explicit, exports are documented.
Data provenance- Building, imagery, label, and release metadata are recorded.
PWTT adaptation- Uses PWTT correctly and addresses WUI-specific masking/vegetation issues.
Validation- Metrics are correct, thresholds are compared, uncertainty is handled honestly.
Error analysis- False positives and false negatives are mapped and interpreted.
Communication- Report and presentation make a clear, evidence-based recommendation.

Project concept
Build a reproducible workflow that divides a disaster-affected area into H3 cells and lets people manually classify Overture building footprints using pre-event and post-event imagery.
H3 should be used to partition, assign, and track work. The annotation unit should remain the individual Overture building, identified by its Overture/GERS ID.
Area of interest
  -> extract Overture buildings
  -> assign each building to one H3 task cell
  -> annotator claims a cell
  -> inspect before/after imagery
  -> label each building
  -> review and export the results
This is a prototype version. It will be limited to one event and one area, with imagery selected in advance.

Core workflow

Select an event, area of interest, and observation period.
Extract building polygons from a pinned Overture release.
Assign each building to exactly one H3 cell using a point guaranteed to lie inside its footprint. Do not assign a building to every cell its polygon touches.
Count buildings per cell and select a resolution that produces manageable tasks.
Present one claimed H3 cell, its buildings, and pre/post imagery to an annotator.
Save each decision immediately and track task progress.
Have multiple people annotate a subset of cells for quality assessment and adjudication.
Export the annotations with enough provenance to reproduce and interpret them.

H3 resolutions 9 or 10 are reasonable starting points, but the final resolution should be chosen using the number of buildings per task rather than area alone. Resolution 9 averages about 0.105 km² per hexagon and resolution 10 about 0.015 km², although actual cell areas vary. See the H3 resolution statistics.
When a building crosses a hexagon boundary, assign it using a representative interior point but display a buffer around the active cell so the annotator retains visual context.

Annotation interface
The minimum useful interface should provide:

A queue of available H3 cells.
A way to claim, release, skip, and complete a cell.
Automatic zoom to the selected cell.
Synchronized pre-event and post-event imagery, preferably with a swipe or side-by-side control.
Clickable Overture footprints over the imagery.
Keyboard shortcuts for rapid classification.
A visible completed/remaining building count.
Undo and autosave.
An export mechanism and an administrative progress view.

Use more than a forced binary classification:

destroyed
not_destroyed
uncertain
not_visible
footprint_mismatch

An optional damage-level field could be added later, but only after students establish a clear interpretation guide with image examples.
Each annotation should record at least:
building_id
overture_release
h3_cell
label
confidence
annotator_id
imagery_source
pre_image_date
post_image_date
annotation_timestamp
notes
Labels should be described as observations made from specified imagery, not as authoritative structural-safety assessments.

Possible implementations
QGIS workflow
QGIS is the fastest path to a working prototype and may be preferable if the learning goal is GIS workflow design rather than web development.
The recommended QGIS version of the project is still a data pipeline plus an annotation project. Prepare the Overture and H3 layers outside QGIS first, then give students a QGIS project that already contains the task grid, building footprints, imagery, styling, and annotation fields.
1. Choose the building time period
.
Overture buildings should be selected by release, not by an arbitrary date range. A release is a snapshot such as 2026-06-17.0; it is not the date on which every building was originally mapped. For disaster annotation, pick and record the release that is the latest release available before 2022-07-22 .
Important constraints:

Do not use “latest” for a class project unless the exact release is recorded.
Overture public release buckets retain only the most recent releases for a limited time, so download and archive the subset used for the course.
If the event is historical and the matching release is no longer public, use an archived copy, a previously downloaded subset, or document that the available Overture release is a proxy for the desired building inventory.
Record the Overture release, schema version, download date, AOI, and query used to create the local file.

For a quick current-release extract, the Overture Python client can export buildings for a bounding box:
overturemaps download \
  --bbox=-120.15,35.20,-120.00,35.32 \
  -f geoparquet \
  --type=building \
  -o data/overture_buildings_latest.geoparquet
For a reproducible pinned release, prefer DuckDB so the release appears directly in the source path. Replace the release ID in the path with the release chosen for the project:
LOAD spatial;
LOAD httpfs;
SET s3_region = 'us-west-2';

COPY (
  SELECT
    id AS building_id,
    geometry
  FROM read_parquet(
    's3://overturemaps-us-west-2/release/2026-06-17.0/theme=buildings/type=building/*',
    filename = true,
    hive_partitioning = 1
  )
  WHERE
    bbox.xmin <= -120.00 AND bbox.xmax >= -120.15
    AND bbox.ymin <= 35.32 AND bbox.ymax >= 35.20
) TO 'data/overture_buildings_2026-06-17.gpkg'
WITH (FORMAT GDAL, DRIVER 'GPKG');
Use the bounding-box predicate first because it lets DuckDB skip remote Parquet chunks. If the AOI is not rectangular, run a second clip in QGIS or add a spatial intersection against an AOI polygon after the bounding-box filter.
2. Load Overture buildings into QGIS
Add the exported GeoPackage or GeoParquet file with Layer -> Add Layer -> Add Vector Layer, or drag it into the QGIS canvas. Set the project CRS to an appropriate local projected CRS for editing and measurement, but keep a WGS84 copy of the building layer available for H3 generation because H3 indexes use longitude/latitude.
Inspect the buildings before building the task grid:

Check whether the footprints line up with the pre-event imagery.
Remove or flag obvious duplicates only if the rule is documented.
Keep building_id unchanged; it is the stable identifier used in the annotation export.
Add fields for overture_release, h3_cell, label, confidence, annotator_id, imagery_source, pre_image_date, post_image_date, annotation_timestamp, and notes.

3. Assign buildings to H3 cells
The cleanest assignment rule is: one building gets one H3 cell, based on an interior representative point. Do not assign a building to every H3 cell that its footprint touches.
One reproducible Python script can create both the building assignment layer and the H3 task layer:
import geopandas as gpd
import h3
from shapely.geometry import Polygon

H3_RESOLUTION = 9
OVERTURE_RELEASE = "2026-06-17.0"

buildings = gpd.read_file("data/overture_buildings_2026-06-17.gpkg")
buildings = buildings.to_crs(4326)

points = buildings.geometry.representative_point()
buildings["h3_cell"] = [
    h3.latlng_to_cell(point.y, point.x, H3_RESOLUTION)
    for point in points
]
buildings["overture_release"] = OVERTURE_RELEASE

def h3_polygon(cell):
    boundary = h3.cell_to_boundary(cell)
    return Polygon([(lng, lat) for lat, lng in boundary])

counts = buildings.groupby("h3_cell").size().rename("building_count")
h3_cells = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {"h3_cell": counts.index, "building_count": counts.values},
    geometry=[h3_polygon(cell) for cell in counts.index],
    crs="EPSG:4326"
)

buildings.to_file("data/buildings_with_h3.gpkg", layer="buildings", driver="GPKG")
h3_cells.to_file(
    "data/buildings_with_h3.gpkg",
    layer="h3_tasks",
    driver="GPKG",
    mode="a"
)
Load both layers into QGIS from the GeoPackage. The buildings layer carries the h3_cell assignment for each footprint, and the h3_tasks layer gives QGIS real polygon geometries for the H3 cells. Style h3_tasks by building_count to confirm that task sizes are reasonable before annotation begins.
4. Alternative: create H3 directly inside QGIS
If students should practice more of the workflow in QGIS, install the H3 Toolkit plugin from Plugins -> Manage and Install Plugins. The plugin adds an H3 processing provider, but QGIS must also have the Python h3 package available.
Useful tools:

Create H3 grid inside polygons: generate H3 polygons for the AOI.
Create H3 grid: generate H3 polygons for the current map extent.
Count points on H3 Grid: convert building representative points into H3 polygons with counts.

The QGIS-only path is:

Run Vector geometry -> Point on surface on the Overture building footprints.
Run H3 -> Count points on H3 Grid on those representative points at resolution 9 or 10.
Save the output as a GeoPackage layer named h3_tasks.
Run Join attributes by location so each representative point receives the containing h3_tasks.index value.
Join that point layer back to buildings by building_id, then rename or copy index to h3_cell.
Verify that every building has exactly one h3_cell.

This is convenient for teaching, but the scripted Python path is easier to reproduce and audit.
5. Build the QGIS annotation project
Once buildings and H3 cells are prepared:

Add pre-event and post-event imagery as separate raster or XYZ/WMTS layers.
Put h3_tasks above imagery with transparent fill and a visible outline.
Put buildings above imagery with categorized symbology for label.
Use a layer filter such as "h3_cell" = '8929a1d75afffff' when an annotator is working on one task cell.
Add a rule-based style for unlabeled buildings so remaining work is obvious.
Configure the building layer’s attribute form with value maps for label and confidence.
Enable editing only on the annotation fields, not on building_id, h3_cell, or geometry.
Save the project with relative paths so the package can be moved between machines.

For single-user or small-class work, each student can receive a GeoPackage containing assigned H3 cells and their buildings. For simultaneous editing, store the same layers in PostGIS and add fields such as claimed_by, claimed_at, completed_at, and review_status to the h3_tasks table.
Advantages are rapid development, strong raster support, offline operation, and familiar editing tools. Weaknesses are distributing updates, preventing duplicate work, merging files, and supporting many simultaneous annotators. A shared PostGIS database can address concurrency but adds administration and makes the workflow less portable.
Google Earth Engine application
Earth Engine is attractive when appropriate pre/post imagery is already in its catalog or has been uploaded as assets.

Upload the AOI, H3 IDs, and an extracted Overture building subset as a table asset/FeatureCollection.
Build a JavaScript Earth Engine App with before/after maps and label buttons.
Use Earth Engine’s UI widgets to navigate cells and switch imagery.
Export completed annotations or send decisions to a separate external database/API.

Earth Engine Apps are easy to share and can be used without requiring every viewer to have an Earth Engine account. Earth Engine also provides map, button, panel, and drawing widgets through its UI API. Its main limitation for this project is persistent collaborative write-back: a separate backend is likely necessary for reliable multi-user task claiming and annotation storage. Large building collections should be uploaded as table assets rather than embedded directly in a script.
Standalone notebook
A Jupyter notebook is a good teaching prototype or single-annotator tool.

Query an AOI from Overture with DuckDB or the Overture client.
Compute a representative point and H3 ID for each building.
Display imagery and polygons using ipyleaflet, leafmap, or another interactive map widget.
Use ipywidgets buttons and keyboard controls to assign labels.
Save after every decision to SQLite, GeoPackage, or Parquet.

This implementation keeps the data pipeline visible and is straightforward to distribute as a reproducible environment. It is less suitable for many annotators because notebooks do not naturally provide task locking, authentication, centralized persistence, or robust deployment. It is an excellent first milestone before moving the same data model into a web application.

Imagery requirements and risks
Imagery is likely to be harder than either H3 indexing or Overture extraction.

Building-level assessment generally requires high-resolution aerial or satellite imagery; Sentinel-2 is usually too coarse for individual buildings.
Pre/post images must have documented acquisition dates and reasonable co-registration.
Clouds, smoke, shadows, seasonal differences, and oblique views need explicit handling.
Overture polygons may be stale, missing, duplicated, or offset from the imagery.
Imagery licensing must permit classroom display and the intended distribution of derived annotations.

For the first course offering, provide a prepared imagery catalog rather than requiring the tool to discover suitable imagery for arbitrary events. If imagery is delivered as COGs, a tile service can provide browser-friendly access without first creating a large static tile pyramid.

Quality assurance

Write a concise labeling manual with positive, negative, uncertain, obscured, and footprint-error examples.
Run a small pilot before opening the full AOI.
Double-annotate a sample of tasks and calculate inter-annotator agreement.
Include an adjudication workflow for disagreements.
Track skipped cells and missing imagery rather than treating them as complete.
Preserve original judgments as well as adjudicated labels.
Test performance in dense and sparse neighborhoods before fixing the H3 resolution.

Licensing and reproducibility
Record the exact Overture release because its data and schema change over time. Overture building data is distributed under ODbL and includes source-specific attribution requirements; consult the Overture buildings guide and attribution guidance before publishing a combined dataset.
The project should also record imagery providers, licenses, acquisition dates, processing steps, software versions, H3 resolution, AOI geometry, and label-schema version.

Suggested team responsibilities

Data pipeline: Overture extraction, validation, H3 assignment, and task generation.
Imagery: catalog preparation, tiling, dates, alignment, and attribution.
Interface and database: map interaction, labels, task claiming, persistence, and export.
QA and deployment: annotation guide, testing, adjudication, documentation, and hosting.

Instructor readiness checklist
Scope and learning goals

Select one disaster event and a bounded pilot AOI.
Decide whether the primary learning goal is GIS workflow design, Earth Engine, notebooks, or full-stack web development.
Define the expected deliverable: prototype, deployable application, or completed annotation campaign.
Set a target number of buildings, annotators, and weeks.
Decide whether students work as one team or as subsystem teams.

Building and H3 data

Select and record a specific Overture release.
Prepare or test the Overture extraction query for the AOI.
Inspect footprint coverage, alignment, duplicates, and obvious omissions.
Choose a provisional H3 resolution and calculate buildings per cell.
Decide how buildings crossing cells will receive a unique task assignment.
Prepare a small development subset that students can load quickly.

Imagery

Obtain suitable pre-event and post-event imagery.
Confirm that its resolution is adequate for building-level interpretation.
Record provider, license, acquisition date, CRS, resolution, and processing history.
Verify pre/post alignment against building footprints.
Decide how imagery will be delivered: XYZ/WMTS, Earth Engine asset, COG/TiTiler, or local raster.
Prepare fallback cells for clouds, missing coverage, or poor-quality imagery.
Confirm that students and eventual annotators are allowed to view the imagery.

Annotation protocol

Finalize label definitions and exclusions.
Include uncertain, not_visible, and footprint_mismatch outcomes.
Prepare example images for every label.
Decide whether confidence and notes are required.
Define when a cell is considered complete.
Define the double-annotation and adjudication procedure.
Clarify that labels are imagery interpretations, not structural-safety declarations.

Technical preparation

Choose the implementation path and provide a starter repository.
Provide a reproducible environment or dependency file.
Provide the annotation table/schema and a small example dataset.
Arrange required accounts, cloud projects, database credentials, and quotas.
Decide where annotation results will be backed up.
Test autosave, recovery, export, and concurrent editing where applicable.
Provide deployment instructions and an instructor-controlled fallback deployment.

Legal, ethical, and operational preparation

Review Overture’s ODbL and attribution requirements.
Review imagery licensing and attribution requirements.
Decide how annotator identities will be represented and protected.
Establish a data-retention and backup plan.
Document limitations, uncertainty, and intended uses of the final dataset.
Identify who will maintain the tool and data after the course ends.

Recommended first milestone
Before building a multi-user application, require each team to demonstrate this complete vertical slice:

Extract approximately 500–2,000 Overture buildings from a pilot AOI.
Assign them uniquely to H3 cells.
Load one pair of pre/post images.
Navigate to a selected H3 cell.
Label and persist at least 25 buildings.
Export records containing full building, imagery, task, and annotation provenance.

Once that works reliably, students can add collaboration, task locking, QA, dashboards, and broader imagery support.

Projections are not perfect

distortions

title: NR 418
text:
Square grids

Conceptually simple
Multiple sets of coefficients needed for analysis due to edge neighbors and node neighbors

Four neighbors share an edge with the focal cell
Four additional neighbors touch only at a corner (node)
Edge and node neighbors are different distances from the focal cell’s center
Analyses must therefore distinguish between edge-only (rook) and edge-plus-node (bishop) neighborhoods

title: NR 418
text:
Icosahedron-based map projections



What the dang is an icosahedron?




What the dang is an icosahedron?

a twenty-sided platonic solid (duh)!





What is a platonic solid?




What is a platonic solid?

merely a convex, regular polyhedron in three-dimensional Euclidean space






image: Isaac Brodsky




  
    
    Your browser does not support embedded WebM video.
  



Animation by Annaaurora, based on Chris Rywalt’s Dymaxion Projection Animation and NASA’s Blue Marble: Next Generation imagery. Wikimedia Commons, CC0 1.0.



A gnomonic icosahedral projection is neither equal-area, equidistant, nor conformal.

Areas become increasingly exaggerated away from each triangular face’s center.
Angles and local shapes are not preserved, except approximately near each face’s tangency point.
Great-circle routes project as straight lines within each face.
Dividing the globe among 20 faces limits the extent of distortion but does not eliminate it.

title: NR 418
text:
H3

H3 is an open source Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index that was developed by Uber.
H3 uses gnomonic icosahedral projection, but…
it does not unfold the icosohedron to make a map,
rather it lays a hexagonal grid on the surface of the faces themselves forming a geodesic discrete global grid system

title: NR 418
text:
Geodesic Discrete Global Grid System


What?





Geodesic

constructed on an approximation of the earth surface, rather than a plane.
“geodesic” describes its recursively subdivided icosahedral structure resembling the geometry used in Buckminster Fuller’s geodesic domes





Photo: Philipp Hienstorfer, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.





Discrete Global Grid System

mosaic that covers the entire Earth’s surface

Workflow

Black plastic separated using SWIR-2
Bare soil pixels separated using spectral slope from 800 – 1600 nm
White plastics distinguished using AVW

Apparent Visible Wavelength
\[
AVW = \frac{\sum_{i=\lambda_1}^{\lambda_{n}} R_{rs} (\lambda_{i})}{\sum_{i=\lambda_1}^{\lambda_{n}} \frac{R_{rs} (\lambda_{i})}{\lambda_{i}}}
\]

AVW reduces the entire spectrum to a one-dimensional metric of color that is correlated to spectral shape
In this paper AVW is applied across visible and SWIR
